html:
A revolt in 1637 and 1638 by peasants, many of them Christian, on the Shimabara Peninsula and the Amakusa Islands in Kyushu, Japan. Its defeat led the Tokugawa shogunate to drive Christianity underground and close Japan to the Portuguese.

The area had been a centre of Christian missions after Francis Xavier. Its new lords taxed it harshly in years of bad harvests and punished Christians cruelly. In late 1637 the people rose up. Their leader was a teenage Christian, Amakusa Shirō, and their banners bore Christian signs.

Some 30,000 or more rebels, with their families, held an old castle at Hara for months against a large shogunate army. Dutch ships fired on the castle at the shogunate's request. When it fell in April 1638 nearly all inside were killed.

The shogunate blamed Christian influence. In 1639 it expelled the Portuguese and ended the Nanban trade, leaving the Dutch at Dejima. Christians who survived hid their faith for over two centuries.
sum: A revolt in 1637 and 1638 by peasants, many of them Christian, on the Shimabara Peninsula and the Amakusa Islands in Kyushu, Japan. Its defeat led the Tokugawa shogunate to drive Christianity underground and close Japan to the Portuguese.
